title: Population-Specific Recalibration, Not Sensor Type or Placement, Determines Wearable Accuracy for Walking Energy Expenditure After Stroke
content: Manufacturer algorithms that estimate walking energy expenditure from wearable sensors show limited accuracy in stroke survivors. This study evaluated whether population-specific recalibration corrects this inaccuracy across three sensors that differ in placement, algorithm and physiological channels. Data recorded during a walking task with indirect calorimetry in adults with post-stroke sequelae were extracted from a health data warehouse. An ActiGraph accelerometer was worn at five placements, an RT6 accelerometer at the hip and a SenseWear Armband on both arms. Each manufacturer algorithm was compared with a recalibrated model built for each sensor by leave-one-participant-out regression on signal and clinical characteristics. An Armband variant added skin temperature, near-body temperature and galvanic skin response. Every manufacturer algorithm performed poorly, with R² ranging from −2.04 for the ActiGraph at the hip to 0.13 for the RT6. Every recalibrated model reached an R² between 0.58 and 0.73, with a mean absolute error of 2.7 to 3.5 kcal. The multisensor Armband variant raised R² from 0.59 to 0.73 at the affected arm but not at the non-affected arm. Population-specific recalibration, rather than the choice of sensor or placement, determined accuracy. Recalibrated wearable sensors can therefore support home monitoring of walking energy expenditure after stroke.
